newsitem.title: USA: Sister's testimony in McVeigh case helps both sides.
newsitem.headline: Sister's testimony in McVeigh case helps both sides.

text.p: By the time she had finished testifying, it was hard to tell which side in the Oklahoma City bombing case Jennifer McVeigh had helped the most.
For the prosecution, the 23-year-old Buffalo, N.Y., college junior had painted a devastating picture of her beloved older brother, accused bomber Timothy McVeigh.

He was, she told the prosecution, a man so consumed with hatred of the government that he had moved from "the propaganda stage to the action stage," roaming the country under assumed names, talking of carrying explosives in a truck and warning, in a letter he wanted her to destroy after reading, "that something big was going to happen."

For the defence, she painted a dramatically different picture -- her brother "Tim" was a patriot who quoted philosopher John Locke, Thomas Jefferson and Henry David Thoreau, a man outraged that government agencies were acting like "fascist tyrants."

Jennifer McVeigh burst into tears -- her only show of emotion in two days of testimony -- when she described how the FBI had treated her shortly after her brother was arrested and charged with the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building.

She told a rapt jury that the FBI questioned her for eight straight days, nine hours a day, without a lawyer present, and had pasted "Wanted" posters of her on the office wall with her photograph -- one taken from her home -- blown up to two feet high.
"They told me that I would be charged with treason. They wrote that the penalty for that was death," she said. Flickers of concern crossed her brother's usually impassive face.
"The FBI told me my brother was guilty and (they) said he was going to fry," she said.

She said she had agreed to testify for the prosecution under a grant of immunity from prosecution even though she maintained she had done nothing, knew of no plot to destroy the Murrah building and did not know her brother was allegedly involved in one until she heard his name mentioned on a car radio while she was on a spring break vacation in Florida.

The news, she said, caused her to "smoke a lot of cigarettes" and prompted her to burn clippings McVeigh had sent her from "The Turner Diaries," a racist, anti-Semitic, anti-government book that features the blowing up of FBI headquarters in Washington by "Patriots" using a fertiliser bomb, the same kind as the one used in the Oklahoma City explosion.

"Both sides got what they wanted out of her testimony," said veteran Denver defence attorney Scott Robinson. "The government got McVeigh the misfit. The defence got McVeigh the patriot and the jury got to hear a tale of government oppression, which will figure large in the defence case."
"She was a tool both sides can use and will," he added.

But he and other legal experts thought the government would utlimately gain more from her testimony than the defence -- although her heart clearly sided with her brother even if her self-interest did not.

The young woman with long brown hair walked into the court and flashed a smile at her brother and then she did her best not to look in his direction. His eyes were downcast during much of her testimony.
McVeigh's eyes stared down at the defence table as his sister told of how he left a message of hate directed against the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco on her computer.
Prosecutor Beth Wilkenson read that message to the court because she said the language was too strong for Jennifer McVeigh to read aloud.
It said in part, "ATF: All you tyrannical mother-f------ will swing in the wind one day for your treasonous actions. ...Die you spineless. cowardly bastards."
